Subscribers can look forward to David Fincher’s 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' starring Brad Pitt, the final season of 'Emily in Paris', and a brand new adaptation of Jane Austen's 'Pride and Prejudice'.

Netflix has officially set a date for one of its biggest 2027 film releases. 'The Take' is a high-stakes heist thriller starring Denzel Washington and Robert Pattinson, directed by the visionary Fernando Meirelles.

The story follows a former Army captain recruited to rob a Manhattan bank where his girlfriend works. Meirelles describes the film as a blend of heist action and psychological drama with a puzzle-like structure that only comes together in the final moments.

2027 is officially bringing FOUR major releases to Netflix, with THE ONE PIECE, BRIDGERTON, NARNIA, and SCOOBY-DOO all preparing to make next year one of the platform's biggest for beloved franchises.

THE ONE PIECE will premiere in February 2027, completely reimagining Luffy's original adventures with stunning new animation from WIT Studio. Meanwhile, BRIDGERTON Season 5 will return with Francesca and Michaela's highly anticipated love story, with filming already completed.

Greta Gerwig's NARNIA: THE MAGICIAN'S NEPHEW will arrive in theaters on February 12 before streaming on Netflix on April 2, exploring the magical origins of Narnia with a cast that includes Meryl Streep, Daniel Craig, and Emma Mackey.

SCOOBY-DOO: ORIGINS is also officially arriving in 2027, introducing a live-action version of Mystery Inc. with Mckenna Grace as Daphne Blake. The series will explore how the legendary mystery-solving gang first came together, including a real Great Dane portraying Scooby-Doo.

From returning to the Grand Line and London's high society to rediscovering Narnia and solving mysteries with Scooby-Doo, 2027 is bringing back some of the most unforgettable worlds in entertainment. Four completely different adventures, one incredible year for Netflix.

🦷 Scientists Develop Special Gel That Could Help Repair Tooth Enamel in Just 14 Days

Researchers at the University of Nottingham in England have developed a promising new approach to repairing damaged tooth enamel using a specially engineered bio-inspired gel.

The pioneering research, led by Professor Alvaro Mata and Dr. Abshar Hasan, was published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal Nature Communications.

The team developed a synthetic gel designed to work alongside the body's natural chemistry, potentially opening a new direction for regenerative dentistry.

Unlike bones, teeth cannot naturally regrow enamel once it has been lost. This is because the cells responsible for producing enamel die before teeth fully emerge, leaving the body unable to replace damaged enamel on its own.

To address this limitation, researchers engineered an organic material using specially designed proteins known as elastin-like recombinamers (ELRs).

When applied to a damaged tooth, the gel creates an extremely thin, microscopic framework that acts as a scaffold for mineral regeneration.

It attracts calcium and phosphate ions naturally present in human saliva and organizes them into structured mineral crystals that resemble the natural composition and architecture of tooth enamel.

According to the research description, this process can produce an organized mineral layer within just 14 days, potentially restoring important properties such as hardness and structural strength.

🔬 A Potential Breakthrough for Regenerative Dentistry
The technology could offer a new way to address enamel damage without relying entirely on conventional restorative treatments.

By encouraging minerals naturally available in saliva to form an enamel-like structure, the approach could potentially help repair early tooth damage and protect weakened teeth.

If further research and clinical testing confirm its effectiveness and safety, the technology could eventually contribute to new treatments for tooth sensitivity, enamel erosion and other forms of dental damage.

However, the research should not be interpreted as proof that people can currently regrow fully lost tooth enamel at home. Further development and clinical validation will be needed before such treatments become widely available.

Nepal Police Deploys 107 Dogs Across 13 Locations, Leo Takes Top Honor This Year

A specially trained police dog named Leo has been awarded the title of 'Best Police Dog of the Year' by Nepal Police in recognition of its important contribution to search and rescue operations during the Bhote Koshi River flood.

According to the Nepal Police Canine Office, Leo played a significant role in searching for people who went missing after a devastating flood struck the Bhote Koshi River on Bhadra 10.

The dog was honored on the occasion of Kukur Tihar, a festival dedicated to celebrating and worshipping dogs in Nepal.

Leo's recognition highlights the important role trained police dogs play in emergency response operations, particularly during natural disasters when locating missing people can be extremely challenging.

Nepal Police regularly deploys specially trained dogs to identify weapons, explosives and narcotics, as well as to assist in search and rescue operations during natural disasters.

According to the Canine Office, Nepal Police currently operates 107 dogs of different breeds across 13 locations nationwide. These dogs are actively involved in criminal investigations and various specialized operations.

Leo's achievement has added another special moment to this year's Kukur Tihar celebrations, recognizing the dedication and contribution of a four-legged member of Nepal's rescue and security teams.

Nepal Deports 86 Bangladeshis in 10 Months as Crackdown on Illegal Foreigners Intensifies
Nepal has deported 86 Bangladeshi nationals over the past 10 months for alleged immigration violations, illegal employment and suspected involvement in criminal activities, according to government statistics.

Bangladeshi citizens are now the second-largest group of foreign nationals deported from Nepal after Chinese citizens.

According to BBC Nepali, 51 Bangladeshi nationals were deported in the four-month period from Shrawan to Ashoj alone. Meanwhile, 18 Bangladeshi citizens are currently being held at the Department of Immigration.

In the latest incident, four Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian citizen were arrested from different locations in Kathmandu on Kartik 16. They were subsequently handed over to the Department of Immigration for further investigation.

Police officials say some foreign nationals have been found entering Nepal on tourist visas but engaging in unauthorized employment. Others reportedly continue staying in the country even after their visas expire or enter through illegal routes.

Authorities are also investigating suspected involvement in criminal activities, including online fraud.

According to police data, a total of 117,682 Bangladeshi nationals travelled to and from Nepal by air over the past year. Of them, 58,879 entered Nepal, while 58,803 departed from the country.

The Department of Immigration says foreign nationals found violating visa conditions are required to pay applicable fees and fines before deportation. In some cases, they are also barred from entering Nepal for several years.

However, officials have clarified that individuals found to have committed criminal offences will face further legal action under the relevant laws.

Authorities are continuing to monitor foreign nationals suspected of violating immigration regulations and engaging in unlawful activities.

From Nepal's Mountains to Global Podiums: Man Kumar Magar's Incredible Ultra-Trail Running Journey

Nepali ultra-trail runner Man Kumar Roka Magar continues to make his mark on the international endurance-running scene, delivering another impressive performance by securing third place in a challenging 100-mile (163 km) race against some of the world's top endurance athletes.

Man Kumar completed the demanding distance in 21 hours, 34 minutes and 34 seconds, earning another international podium finish and proudly carrying Nepal's name onto the global stage.

His latest achievement adds another remarkable chapter to a journey built on endurance, determination and consistent performances across some of the world's most challenging mountain trails.

His success also follows an outstanding victory at the Vietnam Mountain Marathon (VMM) 2026, where he won the 100K category with a new course record, further strengthening his growing reputation in international ultra-trail running.

🏆 A Record-Breaking Victory in Vietnam

Competing in Sapa, Vietnam, in September 2026, Man Kumar delivered an exceptional performance in the Vietnam Mountain Marathon's 100K category.

He completed the challenging 101-kilometre course in 11 hours, 42 minutes and 37 seconds, overcoming more than 5,500 metres of elevation gain to secure first place and establish a new course record.

The demanding competition tested runners with steep climbs, technical mountain trails and difficult terrain across the spectacular landscapes of Sapa.

The route passed through breathtaking mountain scenery, terraced rice fields and traditional ethnic villages, making it a physically and mentally demanding challenge for every participant.

Completing such a demanding course in under 12 hours demonstrated Man Kumar's exceptional endurance, preparation and ability to compete against experienced international athletes.

The Vietnam Mountain Marathon is part of the World Trail Majors series and attracts experienced mountain runners from around the world.

According to the event information provided, the 2026 competition brought together more than 5,300 runners from 54 countries, making his victory even more significant.

🌍 A Proud Member of the Kailas FUGA Team

The real story: A rule published in Mexico's official gazette on October 14, 2026, and in force from October 15, cut the area where gillnets are banned in the Upper Gulf of California from 11,106 to 1,562 square kilometers, an 86% reduction. The government says it follows scientific recommendations and supports fishing communities. Conservation groups say it could accelerate extinction of the vaquita, with only about 7 to 10 left. Source: La Razón de México, published October 15, 2026, with Reuters and Center for Biological Diversity statements.

The vaquita is the world's smallest and rarest porpoise, found only in Mexico's Upper Gulf of California, and gillnets are the main reason its numbers collapsed. On October 14, 2026, Mexico published a rule that sharply changed the map. The area where gillnets are banned shrank from 11,106 to 1,562 square kilometers, an 86 percent cut that took effect on October 15 and reopens roughly 9,500 square kilometers to that kind of fishing.

The government's case: Semarnat, the environment ministry, said the new rule focuses protection on the places where vaquitas have most often been recorded, following recommendations from the International Committee for the Recovery of the Vaquita. It keeps the Zero Tolerance Zone and adds surveillance measures. President Claudia Sheinbaum and Baja California governor Marina del Pilar Ávila said it supports fishing communities such as San Felipe, Golfo de Santa Clara and Puerto Peñasco. Lorenzo Rojas-Bracho, a leading vaquita scientist who took part in the committee, told Reuters he hoped a smaller area could concentrate efforts to save the animal.

The critics' case: the Center for Biological Diversity said Mexico's rules will "accelerate the vaquita's extinction," arguing that the new rule protects the porpoise in only a fraction of its historical range. The numbers behind the argument are small: the 2025 monitoring saw between seven and ten vaquitas, and the conservation agency Conanp reported three sightings in May 2026 outside the Zero Tolerance Zone. It is a decision that two sides describe in opposite ways, and the animal at the center of it numbers fewer than a dozen.

An extraordinary encounter off Newport Beach, California, has brought a rare group of marine mammals back into the spotlight.

On November 3, 2026, whale-watching crews spotted approximately 70 short-finned pilot whales just five miles offshore. According to local whale-watching operators, it was the first documented sighting of the species in the area since 2015.

Despite their name, pilot whales are actually members of the dolphin family. They are highly social animals that travel in close-knit groups and dive deep into the ocean to hunt squid.

Researchers and whale-watching operators believe changing ocean conditions associated with El Niño may have influenced their appearance, although the exact reason remains unknown.

For local whale watchers, seeing such a large group after more than a decade was an unforgettable experience.

The real story: Overnight on November 4–5, 2026, pilot whales stranded on the rugged Ngawi coast near Cape Palliser, in New Zealand's Wairarapa region. The Department of Conservation said at least 20 were stranded, while locals counted up to 50. Four were found alive and two were refloated at the afternoon high tide, but Project Jonah later said all four survivors died. Source: RNZ (Radio New Zealand), published November 5, 2026, with Reuters and NZ Herald.

Nobody saw it happen. Pilot whales came ashore on the Ngawi coast near Cape Palliser, the southern tip of New Zealand's North Island, sometime in the middle of the night on November 4–5, 2026. By morning, local residents found them among the rocks. Two pods had stranded, the second further down the coast. The Department of Conservation counted at least 20 whales; locals said it was closer to 50.

The scene was heartbreaking. Most of the whales were already dead, and ones that were alive were, in the words of local resident Rob Bargh, "on their last breaths." Fisherman Andrew Sim said that in more than four decades on this coast, he had never seen pilot whales come ashore here. A group of people kept the few survivors wet and cool with buckets of water and towels while Project Jonah medics, DOC staff and local iwi worked together. Four whales were alive, and a refloat was planned for the 2:30 p.m. high tide on Thursday.

Two whales were successfully refloated that afternoon, and for a moment there was hope. It didn't last. Project Jonah manager Louisa Hawkes said the four whales that had been found alive didn't make it in the end, including the two that crews had managed to get back into the water. DOC Wairarapa's Ariana Hawira said staff worked with iwi and Project Jonah throughout. As always with pilot whale strandings, the cause is unknown, and rescuers can only say how hard they tried.

An unexpected discovery has brought new hope to scientists studying one of the world's most endangered whale species.

Researchers photographed an unidentified North Atlantic right whale calf swimming beside its 38-year-old mother, known as Silt, near Anticosti Island, Quebec, in September 2026. After analyzing the photographs and research records, scientists confirmed that the young whale had not previously been counted.

The discovery brings the total number of calves identified during the 2026 birthing season to 24, making it the most successful season since 2009.

However, only around 380 North Atlantic right whales remain, including approximately 70 reproductive-age females. Ship strikes and entanglement in fishing gear continue to threaten their survival.

For researchers, finding another healthy calf is a welcome reason for hope.

Source: Associated Press, November 6, 2026.

The real story: Psychologist Christian Frings of the University of Trier proposed in a commentary in the journal Animal Cognition, published September 8, 2026, that orcas off the Iberian coast may keep damaging boats because they anticipate the effect of the action, a boat that stops, rather than out of aggression or revenge. Source: Live Science, published October 27, 2026.

Since 2020, orcas off Spain and Portugal have been ramming the rudders of sailing boats, and by now at least eight yachts have been lost. Theories have ranged from play, to fashion, to revenge for a bad experience. A psychologist now suggests something simpler and less dramatic.

In a commentary in the journal Animal Cognition, published on September 8, 2026, Christian Frings of the University of Trier proposes that the orcas may keep doing it because they learn what happens afterward. In his view, a whale that rams a rudder sees the boat stop, a clear and repeatable result, and the expectation of that effect may be what drives the behavior. Psychologists have studied this kind of learning in other animals. It would also explain why the behavior has spread across a small, closely connected group.

He doesn't claim to have proven it, and he is not describing a grudge. The point of the theory, as Live Science reports, is that it can be tested, for example by looking at how different rudder designs change the whales' behavior. That matters on the water: one thing sailors and rescue officials need is something that works. The orcas themselves aren't talking, but a new idea suggests they may not be angry at all. They may just have figured out how to make a boat stop.

A remarkable discovery has revealed that Southern Resident orcas use pieces of bull kelp as grooming tools to rub one another.

Researchers call this behavior “allokelping.” The whales break off sections of kelp stalks and roll them between their bodies, sometimes grooming family members and whales of similar ages.

Scientists believe this behavior may strengthen social bonds and could provide health benefits by removing dead skin or accumulated fungus.

The discovery was made possible through high-resolution drone photography, revealing an intimate behavior that researchers had not fully understood despite decades of studying these whales.

Even after years of observation, orcas continue to surprise scientists with their intelligence and social behavior.

Source: Puget Sound Institute, October 12, 2026; research published in Current Biology.

A scientific investigation has revealed that a male orca found dead in Scotland may have been much older than researchers originally expected.

The whale stranded on the island of South Uist in 2015. Scientists later examined his teeth using radiocarbon dating, a technique that measures traces of radioactive carbon left by nuclear weapons testing during the mid-20th century.

The results suggested that the male may have been around 65 years old or older, potentially making him one of the oldest male orcas ever recorded.

Researchers from several Scottish institutions participated in the investigation, using the chemical record preserved in the whale’s teeth to estimate his age.

The discovery shows how even the remains of a whale can reveal important information about the lives and longevity of these remarkable ocean predators.

Source: Whale and Dolphin Conservation, November 6, 2026.

An unusual tracking project is revealing the remarkable movements of two killer whales traveling along South Africa’s coastline.

In October 2026, researchers from Sea Search fitted a satellite tag to a female orca known as part of a pair nicknamed Bonnie and Clyde. The tag began transmitting their movements from False Bay near Simon’s Town.

Their recorded journey took them north past Table Bay, Saldanha Bay, and Lamberts Bay toward the Northern Cape. At one point, the pair covered approximately 100 kilometers in a single day.

Researchers described their highly coastal travel pattern as unusual for killer whales in South Africa. By combining satellite tracking, photographs, and biological samples, scientists hope to learn more about their movements, diet, habitat use, and interactions with human activities.

The tracking project offers a rare opportunity to follow the journey of wild orcas across an extensive stretch of the South African coast.

A remarkable sighting off Nanaimo, British Columbia, revealed an unusual feeding behavior among Bigg’s killer whales.

On October 16, 2026, whale watchers observed a male orca known as Lance (T037B1) lifting his tail and moving backward across the surface of the Strait of Georgia. The crew described the movement as a “moonwalk.”

Marine experts believe this behavior may help Bigg’s orcas tear prey into smaller pieces so it can be shared among family members. These whales are cooperative hunters, and sharing food plays an important role in their social lives.

Although the crew did not witness the hunt itself, the whales’ longer dives and tail slaps suggested they may have recently caught prey.

What looks like a dance on the ocean surface may actually be part of a family meal.

He possesses one of the most impeccably polished resumes in modern American political history, yet his road to the Oval Office faces a fierce ideological battlefield.

Pete Buttigieg’s trajectory reads like an intentional blueprint for the presidency. A Phi Beta Kappa graduate of Harvard University, a Rhodes Scholar at Oxford, and a self-taught polyglot capable of speaking multiple languages, he stepped away from private sector consulting to commission as a naval intelligence officer in the U.S. Navy Reserve. In 2014, while serving as mayor of South Bend, Indiana, he deployed to Afghanistan for seven months, conducting counterterrorism armed reconnaissance and convoy driving through hostile territory. Rising from small-town mayor to a breakout primary contender and ultimately serving as Secretary of Transportation, he established a reputation as one of his party’s most disciplined and formidable communicators, regularly stepping into adversarial media environments to debate conservative hosts.

As the political landscape pivots toward the 2028 presidential campaign, Buttigieg stands near the top of nearly every prospective Democratic shortlist. Supporters argue that his calm debate demeanor, executive cabinet stewardship, Midwestern roots, and combat veteran credentials make him the rare unifying figure capable of appealing to suburban moderates and traditional defense voters alike.

However, detractors from both sides of the political aisle present sharp counterarguments. Critics on the right point to supply chain logjams, airline travel meltdowns, and regulatory controversies during his tenure at the Department of Transportation, while skeptics on the progressive left argue that his technocratic style and corporate background fail to resonate with blue-collar workers demanding a disruptive economic overhaul.

Why now? It's a strategy called Agile Combat Employment: instead of packing aircraft onto a few big, well-known bases, the Air Force wants to spread them across many airfields and keep them moving, so an enemy can't knock out US airpower by hitting one spot. The driving concern is China's growing reach and its arsenal of long-range missiles.

The same islands that launched American aircraft in 1945 could soon host US jets again, this time to help deter a war rather than end one.

One grenade bounced onto the small rooftop, landing directly between Carpenter and Eufrazio. There was nowhere to run and no time to kick it away.

On June 19, 2014, Carpenter was awarded the Medal of Honor, becoming the youngest living recipient of America’s highest military decoration for valor.

December 8, 2012. The remote mountains of Laghman Province, eastern Afghanistan.

A team from SEAL Team Six (DEVGRU) completed a brutal 4-hour night march up steep mountain terrain on a single mission: rescue American doctor Dilip Joseph, who had been kidnapped by the Taliban.

As the assault force breached the compound, the point man, Chief Petty Officer Nicolas Checque, pushed through six layers of heavy blankets covering the doorway.

Checque was immediately struck by enemy gunfire and mortally wounded.

Senior Chief Edward Byers was the second man in the stack. With bullets tearing through the entryway in pitch darkness, he didn’t flinch.

Byers sprinted directly into the darkened room, engaged an armed guard with an AK-47, and tackled an insurgent to the ground. While physically pinning the enemy fighter to the wall by his throat, he heard an English-speaking voice call out in the dark: "I'm right here!"

Recognizing the hostage, Byers made an instant decision.

He lunged across the room and threw his entire body on top of the hostage, using his chest, Kevlar, and helmet to absorb any incoming gunfire. While shielding Dr. Joseph with his own body, Byers simultaneously pinned another armed insurgent to the ground with his bare hands until the room was cleared.

Dr. Joseph walked out alive.

Chief Nicolas Checque made the ultimate sacrifice and was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross. Senior Chief Edward Byers was awarded the Medal of Honor.

In the darkest room, under direct enemy fire, real operators don't think about self-preservation. They complete the mission.

Quartermaster 2nd Class Brett Jones joined the Navy at the end of 1993 with one goal: to become a Navy SEAL. He made it, completing two six-month deployments with SEAL Team 8 and later becoming a plank owner of SEAL Team 10, part of a career that lasted almost a decade and earned him several awards and commendations.

He also carried a secret through all of it. Jones served under "Don't Ask, Don't Tell," and he kept his longtime relationship hidden from even his closest teammates. That ended when an accidental "I love you" on an answering machine led to an investigation. He was honorably discharged in 2003, and he has since spoken publicly about becoming the first openly gay Navy SEAL. Throughout it all, he credits the support of his teammates for allowing him to say it with pride.

After the Navy, Jones served as a paramilitary contractor with the CIA's Global Response Staff, working in high threat environments including Iraq. He later told his story in his book, "Pride: The Story of the First Openly Gay Navy SEAL." Today he lives in Alabama with his husband and their son, where he also serves as a part-time police officer.

Are America’s most elite helicopter pilots lowering their legendary standards to survive a military-wide pilot drought?

In a stunning announcement that sent shockwaves through Army aviation, Army Special Operations Command revealed that pilots no longer need a minimum number of flight hours as a pilot-in-command to apply for the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment. For decades, the Night Stalkers required at least 50 pilot-in-command hours and 500 total flight hours — with applicants during the Global War on Terror routinely stacking hundreds more before daring to try out.

Now, that foundational requirement has been wiped away.

The move is the starkest symptom yet of a deep crisis across military rotary-wing aviation. Aggressive commercial airline recruitment has drained the Army of thousands of seasoned warrant officers, peacetime flight hour budgets have steadily plummeted, and the Pentagon is divesting hundreds of manned helicopters to fund uncrewed drone swarms. With conventional aviation units flying fewer hours than ever, younger pilots simply cannot log the cockpit time once needed to qualify for special ops assessment.

While USASOC insists its brutal Green Platoon and multi-year internal training pipeline will protect frontline lethality, veteran aviators are sounding the alarm that the military’s talent reservoir is rapidly running dry.

Does dropping entry requirements allow special ops to build great pilots from the ground up, or is America’s most elite aviation unit being forced to compromise standards due to systemic military neglect?

On November 3, Spokane County Sheriff's Office SWAT rolled out to a home near Spangle, a small farming town south of Spokane, after a wounded woman showed up at a neighbor's door with a gunshot wound. Deputy Mason Acheson and Deputy Parker Perry were hit as they tried to get inside. Their teammates returned fire, dragged them to cover, and started working on them right there.

Mason Acheson, 35, spent eight years as a Washington State Patrol trooper and firearms instructor before joining the Sheriff's Office in July 2022. On the SWAT team, he was a sniper. In uniform, he was a sergeant in the Washington Army National Guard's 3rd Battalion, 161st Infantry Regiment, and had served in Poland. He died the next morning, leaving behind his wife and two children.

Parker Perry, 29, joined the Sheriff's Office in May 2020 and served alongside Mason on SWAT before becoming a K9 handler. His partner, Brego, was with him in Spangle. He was also a captain in the same Guard battalion. Perry was kept on life support so he could give one last gift as an organ donor. He died on November 7, leaving behind his wife, two children, and a third child on the way.

While legislative sponsors argue the statute is vital to shield teenagers from predatory marketing, eating disorders, and unregulated diet pills, the law explicitly flags creatine alongside weight-loss botanical extracts, triggering fierce pushback from fitness enthusiasts, sports scientists, and trade groups like the Council for Responsible Nutrition.

The new regulations place significant compliance hurdles on retailers and delivery services alike. Brick-and-mortar storefronts must mandate physical age checks for anyone who does not appear over 18, and stores are encouraged to place covered products behind counters or in locked display cases. Remote sellers face even steeper barriers, requiring third-party database identity verification during checkout followed by mandatory adult signatures and photo ID inspections upon parcel delivery, with violations carrying civil penalties of up to $1,000 per infraction.

3,800 meters. 2.36 miles. 12,467 feet.

A bullet took nearly nine full seconds in flight before striking its target—shattering the confirmed world record for the longest sniper kill in human history.

The shot was made by 58-year-old Ukrainian SBU counter-intelligence sniper Viacheslav Kovalskyi and his spotter across the Dnipro River in the Kherson region.

At a distance of over 41 football fields, hitting a human-sized target defies conventional ballistic physics:

The Coriolis Effect: Because the bullet stayed airborne for nearly nine seconds, the sniper team had to calculate the physical rotation of the Earth beneath the projectile.

Massive Bullet Drop: The bullet dropped over 300 feet (100+ meters) from apex to impact, requiring the shooter to angle the rifle high into the sky like an artillery piece.

Shifting Winds: Factoring in temperature, barometric air pressure, humidity, and varying crosswinds across two miles of open water and terrain.

The hardware behind the shot was just as extreme: the custom "Horizon's Lord" (Volodar Obriyu) anti-materiel precision rifle, measuring over six feet in length.

In the bottom of the photo, you can see why this rifle reaches where standard weapons fail:

On the right is a standard .50 BMG (12.7x99mm) round.

On the left is the monster 12.7x114mm HL cartridge—a massive 14.5mm anti-aircraft casing necked down to fire a heavy .50-caliber precision match bullet at over 3,400 feet per second, keeping the projectile supersonic far past two miles.

The shot surpassed the previous world record held by a Canadian JTF-2 sniper in Iraq (3,540 meters) and pushed the outer limits of extreme long-range shooting.

To our long-range shooters and snipers: factoring in a 9-second flight time, the Coriolis effect, and crosswinds across 2.36 miles—how much of this shot was pure mathematical mastery, and how much was divine luck?

“IF YOU ARE COMING IN HERE WITH SORROW, GO ELSEWHERE. I AM GOING TO MAKE A FULL RECOVERY.” — Navy SEAL Jason Redman on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most inspirational conversations in the history of The Shawn Ryan Show (Episode #032), wounded Navy SEAL Lieutenant Jason Redman recounted the 2007 ambush outside Fallujah where he was struck by eight rounds including heavy machine-gun fire that shattered his arm and tore away half his face and the legendary sign he taped to his hospital door.

In his own words:

“When I woke up at Bethesda, my face was rebuilt with metal plates, my jaw was wired shut, and my arm was completely shredded.

People would walk into my hospital room family members, friends, senior officers and the moment they looked at me, their faces would melt into pure horror and grief. They would start crying, sobbing, looking at me with this sickening pity, as if my life was completely over.

That look made me sick to my stomach. I was alive. My guys were alive.

I grabbed a bright orange poster board and a black Sharpie, and with my one good hand, I wrote a sign and taped it directly to the front door of my hospital room:

 If you are coming into this room with sorrow or to feel sorry for my wounds, go elsewhere. The wounds I received I got in a job I love, doing it for people I love, supporting the freedom of a country I deeply love. I am incredibly tough and will make a full recovery. If you are not prepared for that, go elsewhere. But if you are, welcome to my room.’

That sign became our line in the sand. You don’t get to mourn me while I’m still standing.”

Jason Redman endured 37 surgeries, extensive facial reconstruction, and years of physical therapy, going on to write The Trident and Overcome and dedicating his life to helping combat veterans conquer their own life ambushes.

Banning pity from your hospital room while your jaw is wired shut and your face is held together with titanium plates is the ultimate definition of the warrior mindset.

Dale Comstock came up the hard way. He started as a paratrooper with the 325th Infantry in the 82nd Airborne before passing selection for the Army's SMU, where he was reportedly one of the youngest operators in the Unit at the time. Over 10 years there, he worked as an assaulter, a master breacher, and eventually a team leader.

In December 1989, during the invasion of Panama, he served as the breacher on Operation Acid Gambit, the hit on Modelo Prison to rescue American Kurt Muse. The assault force landed on the roof, blew their way in, and brought Muse out alive. After his time in the Unit, Comstock moved to 3rd Special Forces Group, serving as a senior NCO and weapons sergeant on an A-Team until he retired in August 2001. Along the way, he wrote 3rd Group's combatives manual and ran the combatives program in the SMU. Outside the military, he also fought as a professional boxer, kickboxer, and MMA fighter.

His story doesn't end with retirement. Comstock later went to work for Spear Operations Group in southern Yemen, where he has been described as head of operations for the team. Drone footage from one of their operations shows him running to a breach point to place a charge he built himself.

Today he's one of three men named in a U.S. federal lawsuit brought by a Yemeni politician who says Spear tried to kill him. The case is ongoing.
Twenty years in uniform, one of the most storied breachers of his generation, and a post-military chapter that's still being written in court.

“DOZENS OF U.S. AIR FORCE REFUELING TANKERS MASS AT ISRAEL’S RAMON AIRPORT: WHAT ARE THEY PREPARING FOR?”

Striking new imagery from southern Israel shows a massive flight line of U.S. Air Force Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers staged wingtip to wingtip at Ramon Airport near Eilat.

While fighter jets and air defense batteries draw the headlines, military strategists know that aerial refueling tankers are the true operational backbone of modern air warfare. Without them, deep-penetration strikes and continuous combat air patrols are impossible.

Key strategic insights behind the heavy tanker buildup:

The Ultimate Force-Multiplier: Fighters like the F-35 Lightning II, F-15E Strike Eagle, and Israeli F-35I Adir carry limited internal fuel. Staging dozens of heavy tankers provides the aerial gas stations required to execute and sustain multi-wave, long-range strikes over 1,000 miles from base.

Why Ramon Airport?: Located in the Timna Valley near Eilat, Ramon Airport offers a massive 11,800-foot runway and expansive apron space, allowing U.S. heavy strategic aircraft to stage outside congested IDF bases like Nevatim while opening direct flight corridors over the Red Sea and Gulf.

Deterrence in Plain Sight: Assembling this volume of refueling capacity in broad daylight sends an unmistakable deterrent signal to regional adversaries that coalition airpower can stay airborne indefinitely.

Round-the-Clock Air Defense: In addition to offensive strike support, continuous tanker rotations allow interceptors to maintain 24/7 loitering orbits to shoot down inbound ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and one-way attack drones.

Do you see this buildup as preparation for imminent joint strikes, or is it a massive display of force designed to deter wider regional conflict?

On August 3, 2026, 255 days into an exhausting marathon deployment aboard the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, 19-year-old aviation mechanic Nicholas McKelvey stepped off the ship and plunged into the Arabian Sea.
He survived 50 minutes in the open water before a search-and-rescue helicopter crew pulled him aboard. In an interview detailing his ordeal with The New York Times, McKelvey described working relentless 12-hour flight deck shifts in blistering Middle Eastern heat, enduring persistent food rationing, and missing the birth of his first child while thousands of miles from home. When asked what drove him to the edge, his answer was direct and heartbreaking — “I didn't want to be there anymore.”
Instead of receiving medical rehabilitation, McKelvey was charged under military law with malingering and unauthorized absence. Following a disciplinary hearing, the Navy handed the teenager a general discharge under honorable conditions on October 29. While avoiding a court-martial, the administrative separation strips him of his post-9/11 GI Bill education benefits, leaving his young family to finance his schooling through student loans.
The ruling has sparked fierce scrutiny over how the military handles sailors pushed to their psychological limit during extended overseas deployments. Navy policy states that suicidal ideation and suicide attempts are medical issues rather than disciplinary offenses, yet commanders retain wide discretion to pursue separate misconduct charges. Documents submitted to Congress revealed that the Abraham Lincoln operated with just six mental health professionals and five chaplains to serve more than 5,000 personnel aboard, during a deployment that saw eight separate suicide attempts across the strike group.
The Abraham Lincoln finally returned to San Diego in October after 322 days away, but Navy leaders have warned that double-pump, 11-month deployments could become the operational norm as global fleet commitments outpace ship numbers.
If you or a service member you know is struggling with mental health or thoughts of self-harm, confidential support is available 24/7 by calling or texting 988 in the United States and pressing 1.
Does discharging sailors who break down on extended deployments protect military discipline, or does it penalize young troops for systemic readiness failures?

They called themselves something close to an "A-Team": a small group of former American special operations soldiers led by Hungarian-Israeli security contractor Abraham Golan. Their company, Spear Operations Group, was incorporated in Delaware in August 2015, and within months its men were in southern Yemen working for the United Arab Emirates during the Saudi-led coalition's war.

According to a federal lawsuit, the UAE paid Spear $1.5 million a month, plus bonuses for successful targeted killings. Its first known operation came on December 29, 2015, a failed attempt to kill Anssaf Ali Mayo, the local leader of the Islamist Al-Islah party in Aden. Former employees have since admitted to the BBC that the UAE provided them with target packets and intelligence. "There was a targeted assassination program in Yemen. I was running it," Golan told BuzzFeed News in 2018. The UAE has denied being behind the killings.

Now the man they failed to kill is fighting back. In 2026, Mayo filed a lawsuit in U.S. federal court against Golan and two former Americans who worked for Spear, Isaac Gilmore and Dale Comstock, alleging they took part in an assassination program that may amount to murder and war crimes.

It's a case that raises hard questions about what happens when special operations skills are put up for sale, and where the line falls between counterterrorism and contract killing.

Michael "Rod" Rodriguez was born into a legacy of warriors.

With a father who fought in Vietnam and two grandfathers who served in World War II, Rod knew his path early. Graduating high school at sixteen, he enlisted in the United States Army at seventeen, joining the 10th Mountain Division and deploying into combat in Somalia in 1993 and later to Haiti.

In 1997, he earned his Green Beret, taking on one of the most demanding specialties in the military as an 18D Special Forces Medical Sergeant and sniper with 7th Special Forces Group.

Over twenty-one years and ten combat deployments across Colombia, Panama, Peru, Bolivia, and Afghanistan, Rod repeatedly put his body on the line. He endured multiple concussions and traumatic brain injuries from enemy blast waves, hiding his symptoms because he refused to leave his teammates down a gun.

In 2013, the physical toll forced him into medical retirement with severe post-traumatic stress and traumatic brain injury.

A bullet took nearly nine full seconds in flight before striking its target—shattering the confirmed world record for the longest sniper kill in human history.

The shot was made by 58-year-old Ukrainian SBU counter-intelligence sniper Viacheslav Kovalskyi and his spotter across the Dnipro River in the Kherson region.

At a distance of over 41 football fields, hitting a human-sized target defies conventional ballistic physics:

The Coriolis Effect: Because the bullet stayed airborne for nearly nine seconds, the sniper team had to calculate the physical rotation of the Earth beneath the projectile.

Massive Bullet Drop: The bullet dropped over 300 feet (100+ meters) from apex to impact, requiring the shooter to angle the rifle high into the sky like an artillery piece.

Shifting Winds: Factoring in temperature, barometric air pressure, humidity, and varying crosswinds across two miles of open water and terrain.

The hardware behind the shot was just as extreme: the custom "Horizon's Lord" (Volodar Obriyu) anti-materiel precision rifle, measuring over six feet in length.

In the bottom of the photo, you can see why this rifle reaches where standard weapons fail:

On the right is a standard .50 BMG (12.7x99mm) round.

On the left is the monster 12.7x114mm HL cartridge—a massive 14.5mm anti-aircraft casing necked down to fire a heavy .50-caliber precision match bullet at over 3,400 feet per second, keeping the projectile supersonic far past two miles.

The shot surpassed the previous world record held by a Canadian JTF-2 sniper in Iraq (3,540 meters) and pushed the outer limits of extreme long-range shooting.

“When I woke up at Bethesda, my face was rebuilt with metal plates, my jaw was wired shut, and my arm was completely shredded.

That look made me sick to my stomach. I was alive. My guys were alive.

I grabbed a bright orange poster board and a black Sharpie, and with my one good hand, I wrote a sign and taped it directly to the front door of my hospital room:

 If you are coming into this room with sorrow or to feel sorry for my wounds, go elsewhere. The wounds I received I got in a job I love, doing it for people I love, supporting the freedom of a country I deeply love. I am incredibly tough and will make a full recovery. If you are not prepared for that, go elsewhere. But if you are, welcome to my room.’

That sign became our line in the sand. You don’t get to mourn me while I’m still standing.”

Jason Redman endured 37 surgeries, extensive facial reconstruction, and years of physical therapy, going on to write The Trident and Overcome and dedicating his life to helping combat veterans conquer their own life ambushes.

Capt. Brian Erickson, a pilot from the 75th Fighter Squadron, was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross with Valor on July 11, 2008.

Capt. Brian Erickson, 75th FS chief of mission planning, earned the medal while deployed to Bagram Air Base, Afghanistan, for providing ground alert close air support to a German Provincial Reconstruction Team that was under nighttime fire from insurgents in a valley of the Hindu-Kush mountains.

"I'm extremely impressed with the way Captain Erickson handled himself out there," said Colonel Kenneth Todorov, 23rd Wing commander, "He provided close air support in hazardous conditions, with no forward air controller and led a successful mission with valor."

On Oct. 16, 2006, Captain Erickson and his wingman, who were then part of the 75th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron, received a short-notice call to provide aerial support to six German soldiers trapped between two mountain ranges. They were receiving enemy fire in the form of rocket-propelled grenades, machine guns, and small-arms fire.

Up until the call, previous flights of non-tactical aircraft had been unable to help the stranded PRT due to their location, limited communication capabilities, and lack of moonlight. Without illumination from the moon or another source, the pilots' night vision goggles provided little assistance.

Once he arrived on scene, Captain Erickson determined there was room for only one aircraft above the mountain tops and just below the clouds. He assigned the safe altitude above the clouds to his wingman, who searched for the insurgents' location with his advanced targeting pod and night vision goggles.

As Captain Erickson flew his A-10 deep into the moonless valley, where the only light on the ground was from insurgent weapons fire, his wingman flew above to relay reports about where the weapon bursts were coming from. Before Capt. Erickson could employ any of his own weapons, he needed to determine the exact location of the PRT to avoid friendly fire.

"I initially had my infrared sensor on to pinpoint the location of the insurgents. The problem with using the infrared was that every time a rocket-propelled grenade went off, the glow impeded my ability to navigate the dark canyon. The whole screen would go white, and I couldn't see outside my cockpit. The only solution was to turn the screens off," said Captain Erickson.

After Captain Erickson turned off his infrared sensor, he continued his low-level runs in search of the PRT. This proved an even more difficult task because the PRT's signaling device, an infrared strobe, was malfunctioning, and the German soldiers, who were untrained in communicating with aircraft, continued to take harassing enemy fire. The chaos of the situation was impaired even more by the PRT's limited proficiency in English. These limitations in combination with the enemy fire caused the PRT to provide confusing information on their exact location.

Realizing that time was running out for the PRT, Captain Erickson released a series of covert illumination flares only visible through night vision devices. Able to "see", he used geographic references from the air and ground to narrow down the PRT's location. During this time, the captain and his wingman were able to identify a location where they believed the enemy fire was coming from.

To be sure of the PRT's location, Captain Erickson conducted a low-altitude show-of-force. He flew between the enemy and friendly positions at 2,000 feet and deployed pyrotechnic self-protection flares, which lit the night sky. His hope was that the enemy would alert to his position and break their attack on the PRT long enough for his wingman to search for clues of the enemy's exact position.

"After we located where we thought the insurgents were, I had my wingman light-up the area with his targeting pod," said Captain Erickson. "During this time the weapons-fire against the Germans was also becoming increasingly accurate, and the need to bring the situation to a close was becoming more-and-more imperative. After we were able to determine that we were, in fact, targeting the insurgents and not the pinned-down German PRT team, it was time to take action."

With Captain Erickson's wingman marking the enemy's position with his TGP's infrared pointer, the PRT confirmed the mark as the enemy fire point of origin. In a single pass, Captain Erickson employed 240 30-millimeter rounds from the aircraft's GAU-8 cannon. This completely halted the enemy's fire and saved the lives of six German soldiers.

Captain Erickson and his wingman remained in the area to monitor both the friendly and enemy positions until the Iraqi National Police and International Security Assistance Force Quick Reaction Force were able to reach and recover the PRT and bring them to safety.

Captain Erickson credited the operation's success to his training. Although he was honored to receive the Distinguished Flying Cross with Valor for "doing the job he's trained to do," he pointed out a higher honor.

"The real reward was returning those six coalition soldiers safely to the village they were working at as part of the PRT team," said Captain Erickson.
